D13 and D24 merged into D4; D15, D29 and D31 merged into D14. Five tombstones, bringing the entry to eight. D4 now holds the contract/build key split — resources, traits and blueprints keyed by their own apiVersion, transformers by the build SemVer — and carries SEVEN alternatives, because this decision flipped twice and both discarded positions were actually adopted rather than hypothesised. Catalog-major keys (D4's own original content) are folded in as originally-adopted-then-reversed with BOTH defects that killed them recorded: reproducibility, since every installed module keyed to @v1 so publishing 1.3.0 changed the transformer bodies every already-installed module rendered against; and granularity, since one namespace per catalog means breaking one trait's shape needs a catalog major bump, so in practice it never happens and 'v1 means v1' becomes unenforceable. Full-SemVer keys plus subscription breadth (D13's content) are folded in as subsequently-adopted-then-reversed, rejected on the cross-catalog coverage failure — the backup/k8up walk is preserved verbatim in D4 because it is the evidence that forced the split and is reproduced nowhere else. D14 now holds the single-build subscription and carries TEN alternatives spanning three adopted-then-reversed positions: the whole-major default (D14's own original content), the prerelease opt-in flag (D15) with its registry measurement intact, and the required non-empty versions LIST (D29) reduced to a scalar by D31. Citation handling was split by kind rather than swept blind, and the first attempt at a blind regex is why: it produced ~25 self-referential sentences ('D29 then removes the list D29 kept', 'D14+D14', 'RETIRED BY D14 ... Under D14') because narrative prose describes the supersession HISTORY, not just the current design. That sweep was reverted and redone as 39 hand restatements plus 62 mechanical renumbers. The rule applied: NARRATIVE documents name the live decision, so the superseded approach is now referred to descriptively ('under the build-keyed contracts D4 replaced', 'the whole-major default D14 originally carried') rather than by a dead number; the DECISION LOG keeps its historical references, which the tombstones resolve, so 'D13 retired D12's catalog lookup' and 'this is D13's own objection to D4' stand as written. Normative references inside LIVE decisions were retargeted (D32's 'After D31' -> 'After D14', D27's 'Under D24' -> 'Under D4', D25, D28, D3, D21), since a live decision stating current behaviour should not point through a tombstone. 162 narrative citations touched across 02-design, README, 04-graduation, 05-risks, 06-operational and schemas/target.cue. The cost this pass accepted, stated plainly: this entry's central decision — the contract/build key split — now sits at D4, a number whose original content was the rejected catalog-major scheme, and enhancement 0011 cites 0010 D24 externally and now reaches it through a tombstone. | [0011](./0011/) | cli | draft | minor | not-started | 2026-07-30 — OQ4 narrowed and OQ8 filed, both consequences of the module having no version at all. OQ4's candidate (b) — the authored version is the sole trigger — is CATALOG-ONLY BY CONSTRUCTION, which the question did not say. Enhancement 0010 D2 deletes #Module.metadata.version, so a module has no authored version available to be a trigger, and the asymmetry compounds rather than being a technicality: retiring publish:smart removes the module fleet's ONLY existing answer to should-this-publish-and-at-what-version, and D3's review seam (`version set` -> diff -> commit -> publish) is structurally unavailable to a module because `--version` supplies the tag directly and writes nothing. So a module's version is decided wholly outside the artifact, by (a) release automation or (c) an advisory checksum, while a catalog may use any of the three; a single mechanism covering both should not be assumed to exist. That also settles half of 04-graduation.md's command-surface gate from the other direction — `opm module version set` does NOT exist, because there is nothing for it to write, so what remains open is what replaces it rather than which command performs it. The gate bullet is rewritten to say so. OQ8 asks whether `--version` means one thing. D3 already gives it two jobs and states the split without weighing it: against a catalog it writes an open identity.cue Version or asserts a concrete one and refuses on mismatch; against a module it names the OCI tag, with nothing in source to agree or disagree with, so the catalog form's refusal path has no module analogue and neither does the value it would write. One flag, two semantics, two failure modes, on a command whose premise (D1) is one pipeline serving both artifact types. Candidates: (a) keep one flag and document the split; (b) take the version positionally for both as `cue mod publish v1.2.0` does, demoting the catalog-side WRITE to the thing needing an explicit flag; (c) split the names, `--version` for the catalog write/assert and `--tag` for the module coordinate. It resolves under the existing command-surface gate rather than adding one, and interacts with OQ1 (what the catalog-side write touches) and OQ4. Neither item changes a decision: D2, D3 and D4 stand as written, and nothing in schemas/target.cue moves. | Module and Catalog Publishing |

| [0013](./0013/) | cross-cutting | draft | - | not-started | 2026-07-27 — Design revised on review: D10 supersedes D1, D11 supersedes D4, D12 amends D9, and OQ1 is closed. D1 had removed the `#Secret` contract type AND the disjunction inside it, when only the routing metadata needed to move to the attribute — leaving the deployer no slot in which to say "this Secret already exists", and forcing the handle-plus-context-map machinery of D4 to compensate. D10 restores `#Secret` narrowed to `#SecretLiteral | #SecretRef`, so the ATTRIBUTE carries routing (author intent, static, in the published module) and the TYPE carries fulfilment (deployer choice, per environment, type-checked by CUE). D11 replaces handle substitution with resolve-in-place: the kernel rewrites every secret to its `#SecretRef` form, so both arms converge before render, a transformer reads two fields from one branch, and the whole handle format, the `#TransformerContext` addition, the `owned` flag and the output scanner are all deleted. Three properties fall out that the first draft lacked: instance files for supplied secrets do not change at all, plaintext in the render is structurally unrepresentable rather than stripped, and a secret interpolated into a rendered string fails at plain `cue vet` at authoring time. Experiment 02 rebuilt as `02-resolve-in-place` and re-run: all five claims held, and its Go content hash agrees with the CUE one in examples.cue. OQ2 opened — whether the arm rewrite survives the real kernel build path — and is now the sole blocker to acceptance. | Attribute-Declared Secret Fields |
| [0014](./0014/) | cli | draft | none | not-started | 2026-07-29 — Drafted. 0006 shipped the handoff that moves an instance's manager to the operator; nothing moves its definition out of the cluster, so a CLI-first user who now wants GitOps hand-assembles four YAML documents per instance from a `kubectl get -o yaml` dump. Three decisions came from the user on the day: the exported unit is the CR plus its apply envelope rather than a bare CR (D1), export refuses to write unless the published module reproduces `status.lastAppliedRenderDigest` (D2, reusing handoff's gate chain and `VerificationDigest`), and `spec.values` is written verbatim with a warning rather than redacted or refused, because OPM cannot yet identify which values are secret (D3). D4 records the live CR as the sole input. Two findings from reading the code shaped the design. `ApplySpec` (cli/internal/inventory/store.go:119) writes only `spec.module`, `spec.owner`, and `spec.values`, so every CLI-written CR lacks `spec.serviceAccountName` and `spec.prune` — meaning a dump-and-strip export applies under the controller's own identity and orphans its workloads on delete, a behaviour difference invisible in the YAML. And the render-bearing / apply-bearing partition resolves the tension that finding creates: the fields the digest gate verifies are copied untouched, while the fields governing apply identity and deletion sit outside the render digest and can be completed without weakening the guarantee, provided every completion is reported. The partition is enforced in schemas/target.cue rather than asserted in prose. Six open questions; OQ4 (field-manager collision when Flux's kustomize-controller applies over fields owned by opm-cli and the operator) is the load-bearing one and is gated on a runnable experiment, because it decides whether the adoption is as quiet as D2's guarantee implies. | Export a Deployed Instance as GitOps Manifests |

## Status legend

- **draft** — initial design, actively being written
- **accepted** — design agreed upon, ready for implementation
- **implemented** — design has been realized in code
- **superseded** — replaced by a newer enhancement (see `superseded_by` in the entry's config.yaml)
